request:
A world in the SIMMONS-TOMB-FIELD sector, kept after Dan Simmons — Hyperion.

The operations this world is built from:
- Reverse Time: a universe where local causal order is reversed (time and causality, distribution).
- Relativistic Dilation: a universe where the traveler experiences years while the outside experiences millennia (time and causality, alteration).

When we arrive: Funerary structures move against the direction of time, and a woman receives forgiveness before committing the act for which she will later need it.

The central tension we want to continue: Kesh can draw the causal diagram, but the diagram does not contain shame and responsibility lived in reverse order

What the course asks of this world: reverse-time SF; relativistic SF.

sourceText: cells: Ti, Dl Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the SIMMONS-TOMB-FIELD sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly. Funerary structures move against the direction of time, and a woman receives forgiveness before committing the act for which she will later need it. The memorial bore the name of Dan Simmons — Hyperion precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Time became truly interesting only when it was taken out of clock mechanics and placed inside law: who is responsible for an act already witnessed, who inherits a temporal copy, and what consent means between persons who do not share the same order of events. Tern had specialized in things that did not answer. In a family built for exploration, he had become the custodian of the right to silence. At the center of the conflict was Aren, an administrator chosen precisely because they were not a specialist in the phenomenon that had reorganized the world. ‘The specialists tell me what can be done,’ 119 they said. ‘I have to answer who it may be done to.’ Kesh kept the distinction in his notes. The problem closed quickly around them: Kesh can draw the causal diagram, but the diagram does not contain shame and responsibility lived in reverse order. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Ti — Reverse Time: local causal order is reversed; Dl — Relativistic Dilation: the traveler experiences years while the outside experiences millennia. Course references included reverse-time SF; relativistic SF. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Kesh broke the first consensus. ‘If the element explains everything, we do not have an element. We have a word that has eaten the problem.’ Orin answered without raising their voice: ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated 120 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Marae remained in the local body when the others opened their protections. The gesture cost her: she felt cold, pressure, and physiological delay at exactly the scale the inhabitants felt them. “Otherwise we risk confusing the fact that we survive with the claim that the situation is bearable,” she said after catching her breath. The night did not end in victory. Orin discovers grief for an act not yet committed that has already left traces. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. While Kesh closed the record, Tern compared the sector’s noise with the anomaly detected in the Vinge zone. The pattern reappeared, but only in worlds where Aster’s control weakened. The correlation was unpleasant: either someone was calling him from outside, or his own need for an outside was learning to forge evidence. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the BOUNDARY operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — moves, perforates, or redefines the boundary between inside and outside — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. 121 Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. Kesh left the cell open. Not because he did not know what to write, but because a provisional classification preserved the possibility that the next world might contradict it. 122 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
